Article Title: Proposed MDR for UPI transactions will be nominal, says government
Article Text:
Government officials have indicated that MDR of 0.25% to 0.4% may be allowed for UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, with a ceiling on the charge.

NEW DELHI: The government said on Saturday that the proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) for UPI transactions will be nominal and apply only to a limited set of merchants for transactions above a threshold, while seeking to assure users that all person-to-person transactions will remain free and consumers who make the payment will not face any fees."A vast majority of the transactions will remain free of charge for merchants on UPI. MDR, if introduced, will only be threshold-based and not levied on a blanket basis to all," the statement said, adding that the UPI and Services Steering Committee, headed by NPCI, will decide on the MDR, if any.It also dismissed reports of the charges being imposed under pressure from the US, which was seen to be pushing the case of Visa and Mastercard that levy MDR on credit card and debit card transactions, which are up to 2%, and usually not passed on to consumers unless the merchant is keen on a cash transaction. "If external pressure had been a factor, the government would not have introduced UPI in 2016 or made it free of charge for both merchants as well as citizens since Jan 2020 and ensured that it became the world's largest real-time interoperable payment system.The amendment should be viewed in the context of the government's broader objective of ensuring that India's digital payment infrastructure remains sustainable, competitive, and capable of serving the country's rapidly expanding digital economy."The finance ministry argued the move was necessary to expand the infrastructure into rural and semi-urban areas. Officials have indicated an MDR of 0.25% to 0.4% may be allowed for UPI transactions above Rs 2,000, provided they are not person-to-person, with a ceiling on the charge.
Article Summary: Government officials have indicated that mdr of 0.25% to 0.4% may be allowed for upi transactions above rs 2,000, with a ceiling on the charge. The upi and services steering committee, headed by npci, will decide on the mdr, if any.

Article Title: 'Power Banks' for satellites? Bengaluru Company builds tech to keep ageing spacecraft alive
Article Text:
Aule On-screen setup running multibody dynamics simulations and tracking system capturing hardware test data for position and velocity for correlation

Aule 2: Dark room hardware test setup where the team recreated on-orbit lighting conditions with a sun simulator and a target mounted on a robotic arm to simulate the target’s motion.

BENGALURU: What if satellites could simply plug into a power bank instead of drifting away when they run out of fuel? That’s the idea driving a Bengaluru startup building “jetpack” satellites designed to latch onto ageing spacecraft, take over their propulsion duties and keep billion-dollar assets working years longer.After recently validating a key part of its technology at an Isro facility used for India’s SpaDeX docking mission, Aule Space is now preparing for what could become one of the world’s most ambitious private satellite docking demonstrations.For satellite operators, running out of fuel doesn’t necessarily mean spacecraft have reached the end of life. In many cases, expensive communication satellites remain fully functional, but can no longer maintain their assigned orbital positions because they have exhausted the propellant needed for station-keeping. Once that happens, operators are forced to retire assets worth hundreds of millions of dollars.Aule has found another way. “We’re trying to build satellites which can go and dock to existing satellites in space which don’t have any installed ports... and extend their life so that they can keep generating revenue,” CEO Jay Panchal, told TOI. “It’s like a power bank,” he added.Instead of attempting the far more complicated task of refuelling satellites in orbit, Aule’s approach is to send a smaller “jetpack” spacecraft that docks with an existing communications satellite and assumes responsibility for station-keeping using its own propulsion system.The company plans to target geostationary communication satellites, many of which cost more than $300 million to build and generate significant annual revenues.The challenge lies in docking with satellites that were never designed to be serviced. Rather than relying on dedicated docking ports, Aule will attach its spacecraft to the liquid apogee motor (LAM) nozzle, a standard external feature found on most geostationary satellites.If successful, the technology could help operators extract years of additional service from satellites that would otherwise become orbital relics. Panchal said each docked “jetpack” could extend a satellite’s operational life by up to 5 years.*Key Test Done*The startup recently completed a major milestone by testing its camera-based guidance, navigation and control system at the Rendezvous Simulation Laboratory (RSL) at Isro’s ISITE — the same lab where critical elements of the SpaDeX were validated.“We were the first non-govt entity to access RSL. This is the best kind of on-ground testing we can do for these capabilities,” Panchal said.One of Aule’s differentiators is its reliance on computer vision instead of multiple specialised sensors. Current docking systems typically use LiDAR, infrared cameras and other sensors. Aule says its spacecraft will perform the critical final approach using a single optical camera powered by onboard AI.The visual navigation models are trained using data generated in its own facilities and validated at Isro’s testbed before being deployed in orbit.The company is targeting an in-orbit demonstration next year, when it plans to launch two satellites that will autonomously dock in low-Earth orbit. Panchal claims it could be the world’s first private mission to perform non-cooperative docking in LEO using camera-only navigation. The mission will validate technologies that Aule ultimately intends to deploy around geostationary communication satellites.
Article Summary: Bengaluru startup building ‘jetpack’ satellites designed to latch onto ageing spacecraft. Aule space preparing for what could become one of the world’s most ambitious private satellite docking demonstrations. Company plans to target geostationary communication satellites, many of which cost more than $300 million to build.

Article Title: Safety vs privacy: How domestic-help platforms are building a two-way support system
Article Text:
A significant demographic of the service providers at these platforms and the consumers comprise of women.

Formalising trust in an informal workforce

Safety vs surveillance divide

Safety by design

What women check before opening the door

The rituals of being home alone

The older customer’s definition of trust

The next phase of trust

India’s instant domestic help economy is expanding faster. App-based platforms promise cleaners, cooks and household workers within minutes. However, the real contest here is no longer just about speed, convenience or pricing. It is increasingly about trust.A significant demographic of the service providers at these platforms and the consumers comprises women.For years, domestic work in India has operated through informal neighbourhood networks, word-of-mouth referrals and personal recommendations. The new generation of platforms is attempting to formalise that ecosystem by adding identity verification, digital payments, ratings, training, insurance and customer support.But unlike food delivery or ride-hailing, these services involve something far more intimate: a stranger entering a private home.That has forced platforms to solve an unusually difficult problem. They must simultaneously protect women who enter unfamiliar homes for work and women who may be home alone when they invite those workers inside.The result is a rapidly evolving safety architecture built around background checks, restricted service hours, real-time monitoring, SOS systems, human escalation teams and, increasingly, AI-assisted risk detection.India’s domestic work sector employs millions of workers, many of them women, and remains overwhelmingly informal. Instant domestic help platforms have created new income opportunities by offering structured onboarding, predictable payments and access to a larger customer base.But formalisation has also brought safety concerns into sharper focus.A spokesperson for Pronto shared the measures it takes to ensure transparency, saying that every worker completes criminal court record verification and police verification before joining the platform. Customers, too, verify their name, phone number and address through OTP authentication and must agree to a code of conduct before placing a booking.Pronto's workers, for example, receive training before taking their first assignment, and that low customer ratings are investigated by trainers rather than triggering automatic deactivation.“Every hub we operate doubles as a training centre, and a professional takes her first booking only after she is trained, background-verified and dispatch-ready, a process that takes about four days,” the spokesperson said.Similarly, Snabbit, whose workforce consists entirely of women professionals, said it has built a multi-layered safety framework supported by a dedicated Trust & Safety team.A spokesperson said the system includes “mandatory KYC and background checks for all experts on the platform, verified customers, address-level traceability and controlled job allocation.”The sharpest divide between platforms and customers is emerging around body-worn cameras.Pronto has begun experimenting with optional recorded bookings designed to protect workers from false allegations in cases of disputes with customers.For many users, however, the presence of a camera inside a private home changes the nature of the interaction. “I know some platforms are starting to equip their workers with chest-mounted bodycams for transparency, and while I understand it protects the worker from false claims, it completely freaks me out as a customer,” a Delhi resident said.“My home is my private sanctuary. The idea of a stranger walking through my living room with an active lens, recording the exact layout of my home, my entrances, my exits, my personal belongings, and where my work setup or valuables are, feels like an extreme invasion of privacy.”Her concerns extend beyond the recording itself. “Where is that video footage stored? Who at the tech company has access to it? Could that footage leak or be hacked?” she said. “I would honestly think twice before booking a service that mandates live video recording inside my private space. There has to be a boundary between physical safety and digital surveillance.”Pronto, however, ensured that the sole mechanism of this process is to ensure safety and privacy.It said that additional video data is collected only on opt-in verified bookings. According to its spokesperson, customers choose the feature during booking and confirm it again when the worker arrives. The camera is tilted downward to capture only the work area, records no audio, blurs faces and personal information on the device itself, deletes raw footage immediately, and retains only an anonymised encrypted version for a limited review period and AI training.One of the most striking trends across the sector is that many safety measures are designed not around responding to incidents, but around preventing high-risk situations from arising in the first place.Several platforms have restricted service hours, particularly avoiding late-evening and night bookings when women workers may be required to enter unfamiliar homes after dark.Snabbit said its safety system monitors active jobs in real time and can identify anomalies that may require intervention. According to its spokesperson, “Active jobs are monitored in real time, with the dedicated Trust & Safety team supporting rapid escalation and incident response.”For many women, however, trust begins long before a worker arrives.A 24-year-old student in Jaipur said she has developed a consistent checklist before booking any on-demand domestic service. She checks whether the app displays a verified profile with a photograph, ID verification, ratings and reviews, and prefers platforms that offer real-time tracking and OTP-based service verification.“The first thing I check is whether the app shows a verified profile with a photo, ID verification, ratings, and reviews from other women,” she said. “Real-time tracking and an OTP-based start and end of the service also make me feel more comfortable.”Before the worker arrives, she follows a set of precautions that have become almost automatic. She keeps her phone fully charged, informs at least one friend that someone is coming over, avoids leaving valuables or personal documents in plain sight, and stays in a part of the house where she can easily monitor what is happening.“I usually make sure my phone is fully charged and I let at least one friend know that someone is coming over,” she said. “If it’s a longer service, I stay in a part of the house where I can easily see what’s happening.”She is also careful about digital privacy. “I prefer apps that mask phone numbers, and I never share extra details unless they’re necessary for the service,” she said. “I avoid mentioning that I live alone or discussing my schedule. Once the job is done, I’m careful not to continue communication outside the platform.”For her, safety is not just about preventing a crime; it is about minimising information that could make her vulnerable later.Minal, a 26-year-old professional in Delhi described a different set of habits that have emerged through repeated use of instant service platforms. While the agent is at home, she stays in the hall rather than a closed bedroom, keeps her phone in her hand, and deliberately leaves a pair of her partner’s or male flatmate’s shoes near the entrance.“I never sit in my bedroom with the door shut. I stay in the main living area, usually at the dining table with my laptop,” she said. “I also leave a pair of my male flatmate’s or partner’s shoes near the entryway. It’s a small mental trick, but it makes me feel less exposed.”She and two close friends have an informal safety protocol built around messaging apps.“I have a private WhatsApp group with two close friends. We have a tacit rule: whenever an instant maid or repair person is assigned, I drop the tracking link, their name, and a quick ‘Expected time: 45 mins,’” she said. “I don’t overthink it, but it gives me a safety net.”When asked what app features actually make her feel secure, she was sceptical of marketing labels.“Honestly, badges and ‘police verified’ tags on an app screen don’t mean much to me anymore. Anyone can upload a document,” she said. “What actually makes me feel safe is seeing a real-time, live selfie of the person taken right when they accept the job, matching the photo on their profile. Plus, knowing there’s a strict OTP entry system where they can’t start billing until I give them a code at the door.”Her distinction is important: she is less interested in historical verification and more interested in real-time authentication.For older users, digital verification often feels less persuasive than physical verification. Sarita , a 52-year-old homemaker in Delhi-NCR, said she places greater trust in tangible indicators such as uniforms, identity cards and residential security systems.“A professional now gets to share her version of events and any relevant information before a decision is taken, and we work to keep investigations balanced and transparent,” Pronto spokesperson said.That shift, from treating workers merely as service providers to treating them as rights-bearing participants in the platform ecosystem, may prove as important as any technological innovation.As instant domestic help services expand beyond metropolitan cities into smaller urban centres, safety may become the industry’s primary competitive differentiator.Speed is easy to advertise. Trust is harder to build.Women are asking for features that combine digital verification with human accountability: live identity confirmation, female-worker filters, trusted-contact notifications, residential gate integration, discreet exit mechanisms, neighbourhood-level reputation and transparent data governance.Platforms, meanwhile, are investing in training hubs, background verification, restricted service hours, SOS networks, counselling, insurance and AI-assisted monitoring.
Article Summary: India’s domestic work sector employs millions of workers, many of them women. Instant domestic help platforms have created new income opportunities by offering structured onboarding, predictable payments and access to a larger customer base. But formalisation has also brought safety concerns into sharper focus.

Article Title: IT ministry asks Meta to revamp algorithms, submit roadmap to tackle deepfakes
Article Text:
Meta officials arrive at the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting to meet Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on the issue of the deletion of PM Modi's video message to students from Facebook.

Meta asked to strengthen content moderation

Meta outlines technical measures

Meta under growing government scrutiny over CSAM

NEW DELHI: The ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) has asked Meta to revamp its algorithms and submit a compliance roadmap aimed at curbing deepfakes, propaganda and other manipulated or illegal content on its platforms.The directive was issued during recent discussions between MeitY officials and Meta, amid growing concerns over the spread of synthetic and manipulated content online, ANI cites.Officials have asked the social media giant to strengthen its content moderation systems and act faster on takedown requests from authorised government agencies, the sources said.MeitY also sought greater compliance with data-localisation requirements and asked Meta to work more closely with government agencies to speed up the identification and removal of deepfakes, morphed images and misleading posts.The government has also pushed for specific algorithmic changes to limit the reach and amplification of propaganda and manipulated media.The directive followed talks in which Meta acknowledged gaps in its existing systems and outlined technical measures it could take to address deepfakes and other synthetic content, the sources said.During a meeting with MeitY officials on Friday, Meta's technical team explained how the company currently detects and handles harmful content on its platforms.Officials, however, pressed for more concrete changes to the algorithms governing the spread of such content and sought a clear compliance roadmap from the company.Both sides agreed to continue discussions on the issue, with another meeting expected next week, ANI reports.The government's scrutiny of Meta has intensified in recent days over concerns surrounding deepfakes, Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) and other harmful content on its platforms. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg had earlier apologised over errors related to CSAM and deepfake content after concerns were raised by the Indian government.The latest discussions come as India has tightened its regulatory framework for synthetically generated content, including through amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules earlier this year. The revised rules introduce additional due-diligence requirements for online intermediaries and seek greater accountability for AI-generated and manipulated content.
Article Summary: The ministry of electronics and information technology (meity) has asked meta to revamp its algorithms and submit a compliance roadmap. The directive was issued during recent discussions between meity officials and meta. It comes amid growing concerns over the spread of synthetic and manipulated content online.

Centre has asked Meta to take action against deepfake content, while it examines whether the social media giant is complying with intermediary provisions under Indian law, sources told PTI.A legal opinion on further action is expected after the government reviews the outcome of its meetings with the company.Centre is likely to seek responses from other social media platforms as it examines whether they meet the definition of intermediaries under the country's law, sources said.Sources also said that if Meta and other social media platforms exercise control over what content is shown to users, their role could be viewed as akin to 'publishing', making them responsible for the content and actions on their platforms.The development comes a day after the government held technical discussions with the social media giant, during which Meta outlined its plans to address the Centre’s concerns over deepfakes, child sexual abuse material and unlabelled synthetically generated content on its platforms, sources said.The technical discussions followed two days of meetings in which IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw questioned Meta’s team, led by global affairs head Joel Kaplan, over its content recommendation algorithms and compliance with Indian laws.During the third round of talks, Meta explained how its systems operate and presented proposed measures to tackle the concerns raised by the government. The company said it had solutions to address deepfakes, CSAM and bot accounts, and explained how the measures could be deployed on its platforms, the sources said.Sources had earlier said Meta acknowledged that there were "serious issues" and assured the government that it would take continuous steps to address them. The government, meanwhile, will continue to push the company to undertake sustained measures and improvements to address its concerns, they added.Meta’s global team met IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw and IT Secretary S Krishnan on both days after the government summoned the company over the temporary restriction of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook post.During Thursday’s meeting, the Meta team was questioned on its compliance with Indian laws, content recommendation algorithms and the safeguards in place to ensure that constitutional and legal requirements are met.The social media giant assured the government that it was taking the concerns seriously and was "working hard" to address issues related to deepfakes, child sexual abuse material, bot accounts and synthetic content.On Wednesday, Meta apologised for the temporary removal of PM Modi’s post and acknowledged failures related to child sexual abuse content and deepfakes, as well as the promotion of certain content after being paid "a lot of money".

Article Title: When ‘healthy’ is just a label
Article Text:
.

“Natural”, “healthy”, “organic”, “heart-friendly”, “high protein” and “zero maida” often persuades a shopper before the packet is even turned over. In a spate of notices sent in the past month, Food Safety and Standards Authority of India ( FSSAI ) has asked several brands whether their front-of-pack promises say more than the product can support.FSSAI has issued notices to food businesses across categories including breads, chocolates, juices, cooking oils, noodles, supplements, packaged water and caffeinated drinks. The claims questioned range from “100% natural” and “organic” to immunity, detoxification, disease reduction and energy-boosting promises. Since these are notices rather than final rulings, the issues remain subject to the companies’ replies and regulatory examination. TOI reached out to FSSAI over e-mail, but was yet to receive a response.The scrutiny comes as India’s health-and-wellness food market expands and brands compete for shoppers seeking healthier choices. Experts say the front of a packet increasingly functions as advertising, while the information needed to judge the product — ingredients, sugar, fat, sodium and additives — is usually on the back.Former FSSAI CEO Pawan Kumar Agarwal says consumers rarely read or fully understand the mandatory information panel.Marketing teams therefore have a powerful incentive to foreground attractive words, sometimes stretching the meaning permitted by regulation. For large companies, he argues, penalties may need to be linked to turnover or the commercial gain from a misleading claim rather than treated as a routine cost.Nutrition experts call this the “health halo” effect: one positive phrase can make the entire product appear healthier and reduce the buyer’s inclination to examine it critically. A packet labelled “natural” can still be high in sugar or sodium. “Sugar-free” does not automatically mean low-carbohydrate. “Organic” requires certification; it is not merely a lifestyle description. Disease-treatment or prevention claims require scientific and regulatory support.AIIMS dietician Monita Gahlot advises shoppers to start with the ingredient list, which records ingredients in descending order by weight. The nutrition panel should then be checked for total and added sugars, saturated and trans fats, sodium, protein and carbohydrates. Serving sizes deserve particular attention: a modest-looking number can be based on a portion far smaller than what people normally consume.The clearest warning sign, food-testing expert Ashwin Bhadri says, is a bold front claim that is not supported or adequately explained elsewhere on the label. The simplest consumer rule is therefore to turn the packet over before deciding.Food author Krish Ashok argues that companies are not acting in a vacuum. Consumers increasingly seek a purchasable shortcut to good health. Products labelled “high protein”, “low GI”, “A2” or “heart-healthy” can offer the feeling of making a healthy choice without the slower work of eating fewer ultra-processed foods, increasing fibre and protein, exercising and sleeping well.That is why tighter enforcement alone will not end the health halo. Brands must make precise, evidence-backed claims, but consumers must also stop treating the front of a packet as nutritional advice.
Article Summary: Fssai has issued notices to food businesses across categories including breads, chocolates, juices, cooking oils, noodles, supplements, packaged water and caffeinated drinks. The claims questioned range from “100% natural” and “organic’ to immunity, detoxification, disease reduction and energy-boosting promises.

Article Title: 17.4 lakh blood components discarded in 2025 despite record collection
Article Text:
India discarded over 17.4 lakh blood components in 2025

NEW DELHI: India discarded over 17.4 lakh blood components in 2025, even as blood collection reached a record 1.58 crore units, according to state-wise data tabled in the Rajya Sabha, highlighting continued challenges in blood inventory management despite a steady rise in donations.Available official data indicate that China and India are among the world's largest blood collection programmes. In 2025, India collected 15.71 million units of blood, while China collected 25.5 million units, according to China's National Health Commission.The data, reported by blood centres through the government's e-Raktakosh portal, show that expiry was the leading reason for discarding blood components, followed by reactive units and other operational reasons. Reason-wise discard data has been captured on the portal since 2024, while such details were not available for 2023.Replying to a question in Parliament, the Union health ministry, however, said it had not received any report of regional blood shortages. It added that ensuring an adequate supply of safe blood and minimising wastage is primarily the responsibility of state governments and Union Territories, while the Centre advocates a hub-and-spoke model under which blood is collected and processed at high-volume centres before being distributed to smaller blood banks and storage centres.According to the data, Uttar Pradesh recorded the highest blood collection in 2025 with 21.6 lakh units, followed by Maharashtra (18.73 lakh), Gujarat (11.82 lakh), Rajasthan (10.79 lakh) and Tamil Nadu (9.74 lakh). Overall blood collection increased from 1.42 crore units in 2023 to 1.58 crore units in 2025.The annexure also showed a corresponding increase in blood component utilisation, with Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Rajasthan reporting the highest utilisation during 2025.At the same time, Uttar Pradesh reported the highest discard of blood components at 2.40 lakh, followed by Maharashtra (1.87 lakh), Kerala (1.44 lakh), Rajasthan (1.21 lakh) and Tamil Nadu (1.09 lakh). The ministry did not provide an analysis of the wide variation in discard across states.Dr Hema Goyal, Consultant (Blood centre & Lab services), Aakash healthcare said blood wastage is inevitable to some extent, particularly because platelets have a shelf life of only five days. But discarding 17.4 lakh blood components in a year points to a mismatch between collection and actual demand. The solution is not fewer donations but smarter inventory management through real-time stock sharing and better coordination between blood banks.
Article Summary: India discarded over 17.4 lakh blood components in 2025. Blood collection reached a record 1.58 crore units, state-wise data tabled in rajya sabha. Expiry was the leading reason for discarding blood components, followed by reactive units.

NEW DELHI: In a fresh crackdown on food safety violations, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has acted against two food products, penalising the manufacturer of a fortified sunflower oil after it was found to be substandard and stopping the sale of a Monk Fruit Sweetener over alleged licensing and labelling violations.The regulator imposed a penalty on AWL Agri Business Ltd, Mangaluru, after a laboratory analysis of a retail sample of Fortune "Fryola" Refined Sunflower Seed Oil found that its vitamin D content was below the prescribed standard, making the fortified edible oil substandard under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.FSSAI said the company was given an opportunity to present its case, but the adjudicating authority concluded that it had manufactured and marketed a substandard fortified edible oil before imposing a monetary penalty.In a separate action, the regulator prohibited the sale of PIE Foods' Monk Fruit Sweetener, a natural zero-calorie sugar substitute, after inspections found cartons of the product stored at the company's premises without the required manufacturing licence.FSSAI also alleged that the product carried claims such as "100% Monk Fruit Extract" and "Natural Ingredients", while its online listing did not carry the mandatory endorsement required under food safety regulations.It further said the company failed to produce records showing that the monk fruit extract used in the product had been procured in accordance with the Food Safety and Standards Act.The prohibition order will remain in force until the product complies with the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act and related regulations.The regulator said the actions are part of its ongoing drive to tighten enforcement against food business operators and ensure that products sold to consumers meet prescribed safety and quality standards.
Article Summary: The food safety and standards authority of india (fssai) has acted against two food products. The regulator penalised the manufacturer of a fortified sunflower oil after it was found to be substandard. It also stopped the sale of a monk fruit sweetener over alleged licensing and labelling violations.

Final selection: An expert panel will assess the final proposals using four criteria: Transformative Ambition, Viability, Evidence of Results, and Durability. The winners will be announced in autumn 2027.

Growing reliance on private philanthropy

What the funding could mean

Billionaire Michael Moritz and his wife, artist Harriet Heyman, are offering up to $150 million for ideas that could improve life in San Francisco, launching a global competition to address the city's housing affordability crisis and post-pandemic economic decline.The open competition, called "Boundless San Francisco," was announced on Wednesday by Crankstart, the private family foundation run by Moritz and Heyman. Up to three winning organisations will receive between $10 million and $50 million each to carry out their proposals, according to an official statement from the foundation and reporting by Bloomberg.Any organisation from anywhere in the world can submit a proposal, regardless of the topic, as long as the project directly benefits San Francisco residents."The best ideas rarely come from where you expect them," Moritz, 71, said in an emailed statement.Organisers are running the competition with Lever for Change, a non-profit organisation that connects philanthropists with community projects. Lever for Change has previously managed large funding competitions, including grants to help revive South Side Chicago and expand mental health services across Texas, overseeing more than $2.6 billion in awards to date.Crankstart Chief Executive Officer Missy Narula said the global competition reflects the high-risk, high-reward approach used in venture capital investing. Moritz, a former Sequoia Capital partner born in Wales and knighted in 2013, built his fortune by investing in technology companies such as Google, YouTube and PayPal Holdings Inc.The competition will follow a multi-stage review process before the final funding is awarded:San Francisco has increasingly relied on private funding from wealthy residents to fill gaps in public services. Mayor Daniel Lurie, a former non-profit executive and Levi Strauss heir, has often worked with local technology and finance leaders to secure private support for public projects, including downtown events funded by cryptocurrency billionaire Chris Larsen.Moritz has lived in San Francisco for more than 40 years and has given significant funding to local projects. Bloomberg calculations based on public records show Crankstart has donated more than $1 billion to regional non-profits, academic scholarships, art museums and healthcare providers since 2020.In June, Crankstart pledged $9.2 million to tackle illegal waste dumping in nearby Oakland after local voters rejected a tax measure that would have paid for cleanup crews.Moritz has also supported the San Francisco Standard local news site, funded political ballot measures, and invested in California Forever, a project aimed at building a planned city in Solano County near the Bay Area.The competition could give San Francisco community organisations an opportunity to test ideas that might struggle to secure traditional public funding. Proposals could focus on affordable housing, homelessness, public safety, transportation, education, climate resilience or revitalising vacant spaces, provided they primarily benefit city residents. Organisers say the goal is not only to fund ambitious concepts, but also to support plans that can survive beyond the initial grant. Finalists will receive development funding and technical assistance before the winners are selected, allowing applicants to strengthen their proposals and demonstrate how their ideas could produce measurable, lasting improvements for San Francisco, according to Bloomberg.

Proposals could focus on affordable housing, homelessness, public safety, transportation, education, climate resilience or revitalising vacant spaces.

Article Title: Person-to-person transactions to remain free: Govt clarifies no charges for UPI users - top points
Article Text:
The government said that the overwhelming majority of merchant transactions on UPI will continue to remain free.

Fee on UPI transactions: What the government has said

Who pays for your UPI?

Why MDR may be introduced

External pressure to levy MDR? Government clarifies

Will your UPI transactions soon be chargeable? That’s the question on the minds of users since a bill cleared Lok Sabha allowing banks to charge merchants with a fee. However, the government has clarified that Unified Payments Interface or UPI transactions will continue to be free for users.In a press release, the Ministry of Finance has said that users will not be charged for making UPI payments, and all Person-to-Person (P2P) transactions will continue to remain free.It said that if a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) is introduced in the future, it will apply only to a limited category of merchant transactions above a specified threshold and will be levied at a nominal rate, which will be significantly lower than the MDR that is applicable on debit and credit card transactions.Reports suggest that the government may permit banks and payment service providers to levy an MDR of 0.25% to 0.4% on UPI payments exceeding Rs 2,000 when the transaction is made to a business.As a result, routine payments such as those for milk, vegetables, groceries, auto-rickshaw rides and taxi fares are not expected to be affected.Explaining the rationale behind the amendment to the Payment and Settlement Systems Act (PSS Act), the government said recent changes have been incorrectly interpreted by some as a proposal to levy charges on ordinary users.It said the amendment is an enabling provision intended to support the long-term sustainability of UPI while strengthening its technological capabilities and resilience against emerging risks.The government said that the overwhelming majority of merchant transactions on UPI will continue to remain free. Any MDR, if introduced, will be threshold-based rather than imposed across all transactions.The "UPI and Services Steering Committee", chaired by NPCI, will determine whether any MDR should be levied only after Parliament passes the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, which proposes changes to Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.According to the government, the rapid growth in UPI transaction volumes has made continuous investment in cybersecurity, fraud prevention and infrastructure essential.It also said greater competition requires more companies to expand their presence in the ecosystem, which in turn needs a sustainable revenue model.Relying solely on subsidies would not be sufficient to support the next phase of growth, making a balanced framework necessary to ensure UPI remains robust, inclusive and future-ready.It also said India is entering the next phase of digital payments growth, making it essential for the UPI ecosystem to become financially self-sustaining and affordable as it expands further into rural and semi-urban areas.Earlier this week, RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra said consumers already bear the cost of UPI transactions through the broader economy, even though merchant charges are not levied directly on them.Speaking at a press conference on the proposal to enable merchant fees on UPI transactions, Malhotra said it was too early to comment on the issue, adding that the immediate priority is to further strengthen the payments infrastructure.“It is very premature right now. Now, costs have to be paid by someone - it’s a public [good]; we all want this particular infrastructure to continue to strengthen, become more efficient. That’s our focus as of now - let’s watch how developments proceed,” he said.The government also rejected reports suggesting that changes to the policy were influenced by external pressure, describing such claims as unfounded, false and misleading.The Congress on Thursday had criticised the government over the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, questioning whether PM Narendra Modi intends to weaken the UPI framework and allow US companies greater access to India's digital payments sector "under pressure" from his "good friend Donald Trump".Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the latest Bill introduced by the Modi government removes the legal safeguard that ensures UPI transactions remain free of charge.The Ministry of Finance has clarified that if outside influence had played any role, India would neither have launched UPI in 2016 nor kept the platform free for both merchants and citizens since January 2020, while building it into the world's largest real-time interoperable payment system.UPI handles billions of transactions every month. In July 2026, UPI processed 2,366 crore transactions with a total value of Rs 29.9 lakh crore, making it the world's largest real-time payment system. The platform is now operational in 11 countries, with several more expressing interest in adopting it.
Article Summary: The government said that the overwhelming majority of merchant transactions on upi will continue to remain free. Any mdr, if introduced, will be threshold-based rather than imposed across all transactions. The "upi and services steering committee" will determine whether any mdr should be levied only after parliament passes the taxation and other laws (amendment) bill.

Article Title: Scientists use AI to create new viruses; bringing worries of the tech creating biological weapons, deadly poisons and unstoppable pandemics
Article Text:
An atomic reconstruction of one of the bacteriophages designed by the Evo AI model. (Image credit: Samuel H. King et al.)

How AI learned to write DNA like it writes sentences

How scientists confirmed the AI-designed viruses were actually alive

What the researchers did to keep this from going wrong

The gap between what AI can do and what anyone regulates

Poll Vote & Share your view What fascinates you most about AI designing organisms? Potential for medical breakthroughs The technology behind it The ethical implications The novelty of the concept 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Scientists have used artificial intelligence to design viruses that exist nowhere in nature, and 16 of them turned out to be fully functional killers of bacteria. The work, published Thursday in the journal Science by a team at Stanford University and the Arc Institute in California, is the first time an AI model has written the complete instruction manual for a living thing rather than just one piece of it. The viruses in question only attack bacteria and cannot infect people, animals or plants.That last bit is the reassuring part, and everyone involved knows how thin it sounds. The same study that promises a new weapon against superbugs also proves that software trained on DNA can now dream up a working virus from a blank page. Two researchers at Johns Hopkins, Thomas Inglesby and Moritz Hanke, put it plainly in a commentary published alongside it: the ability to write viral genomes with AI now exists, and the rules to control it do not.The models, called Evo 1 and Evo 2, work a lot like ChatGPT. ChatGPT guesses which word comes next. Evo guesses which chemical letter comes next in a strand of DNA, which uses an alphabet of just four letters: A, C, G and T. Feed it enough genetic code and it starts picking up the grammar of life the way a chatbot picks up English.The team, led by Stanford's Brian Hie, trained it on millions of natural genomes, then focused it on one very well-studied virus called ΦX174 and its relatives.Evo spat out hundreds of thousands of possible designs. The researchers picked around 300, had the DNA physically made in a lab, and slipped it into bacteria—which obediently read the instructions and built the viruses themselves.Graduate student Samuel King spotted it in the early hours of the morning. Bacteria growing on a petri dish form a cloudy film, and when a virus is chewing through them, clear spots appear. The spots appeared. When he told the rest of the team, Hie recalls, "the room spontaneously burst into applause."The 16 that survived were not weak imitations. Some multiplied faster than the natural virus they were modelled on. And in the most useful result of the lot, a mix of the AI-designed viruses wiped out E. coli that had already learned to resist the natural version. A comparable mix of viruses collected from nature could not. Bacteria evolve to survive whatever we throw at them—this suggests we can now design new threats faster than they can adapt.They kept anything dangerous out of the training data. No viruses that infect humans, animals, plants or fungi went in, so the model has never seen what a human pathogen looks like. They used a harmless strain of E. coli and worked in a secure lab. Hanke called the caution commendable, while noting the team had no official rulebook to follow.A new US health policy issued last week bans making biological agents more dangerous, but it doesn't cover work done on a computer. And Evo 2 is open source, free for anyone to download, which has alarmed plenty of people.Others say the panic is early. Tom Ellis at Imperial College London called this the smallest, simplest genome anyone could have attempted. Size backs him up: this virus needs about 5,400 letters of code. The simplest living cell needs 500,000. Hie says going bigger would be "a lot of work, but not impossible"—which isn't exactly comforting.
Article Summary: Scientists have used artificial intelligence to design viruses that exist nowhere in nature. 16 of them turned out to be fully functional killers of bacteria. The work is the first time an ai model has written the complete instruction manual for a living thing. The viruses in question only attack bacteria and cannot infect people, animals or plants.

Article Title: Astrobase unveils 800kN rocket engine, eyes reusability
Article Text:
Astrobase unveils India's first privately-built 800kN full-flow staged combustion rocket engine 'Everest', aiming for reusable launch systems and domestic launch infrastructure.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

BENGALURU: Space start-up Astrobase Space Technologies Friday unveiled what it described as India’s first privately built “800kN Full-Flow Staged Combustion (FFSC) liquid oxygen-methane rocket engine, named ‘Everest’”, as it seeks to develop reusable launch systems and expand domestic launch infrastructure.The Bengaluru-based company said the engine is designed for medium-lift launch vehicles and forms part of its long-term plan to build an integrated launch ecosystem covering propulsion, manufacturing, testing and launch operations. The next major milestone for the programme will be a full-engine hot-fire test, followed by vehicle integration and orbital launch development.According to the company: “Everest uses the full-flow staged combustion cycle, one of the most complex rocket engine architectures, and is powered by liquid oxygen and methane. The engine has been designed for reusability and offers 800 kN of thrust, a specific impulse of around 340 seconds and a throttle range of 50% to 110%.”The company said it plans to manufacture up to 50 engines annually once its facilities are fully operational, with the capability to hot-fire about one engine every week. It aims to test around 20 engines before attempting its first orbital mission.Its first phase of expansion is intended to support about 100 tonnes of annual launch capacity, with a longer-term goal of exceeding 1,000 tonnes through a higher launch cadence.It also said it was “working towards a launch-on-demand capability that could enable a dedicated mission within 15 days of an urgent national requirement. These targets are yet to be demonstrated”.Astrobase co-founder Neeraj Khandelwal said the engine was intended to establish an industrial capability rather than serve only as a technology demonstrator, adding that India would require indigenous high-thrust propulsion systems as satellite launches increase globally.IN-SPACe director (technical) Rajeev Jyoti said Astrobase was among the recipients of IN-SPACe’s Technology Adoption Fund, which is supporting development of the 800 kN engine. He said the programme, as it progresses through development and testing, could contribute to India’s launch capability and create new opportunities in the global space economy.Founded in 2024, Astrobase is developing propulsion systems, test infrastructure and reusable launch technologies from its Bengaluru base.
Article Summary: Astrobase unveils india's first privately-built 800kn full-flow staged combustion rocket engine 'everest' the engine is designed for medium-lift launch vehicles and forms part of its long-term plan to build an integrated launch ecosystem covering propulsion, manufacturing, testing and launch operations.

Article Title: US judge compares Meta to 'public nuisance,' orders $567m payout over child harm
Article Text:
US judge has ordered Meta to pay $567m in a New Mexico child safety case, ruling that Instagram and Facebook exposed children to harmful content and sexual exploitation

India is facing its own Meta child-safety concerns

Meta has been ordered to pay another $567 million by a US judge over allegations that its social media platforms exposed children to harmful content and failed to adequately protect young users.The ruling by Judge Bryan Biedscheid adds to mounting legal and regulatory pressure on Meta over the way Instagram and Facebook are designed and how they protect children from harmful content, sexual exploitation and potentially addictive use.The judge described Meta as a “public nuisance”, comparing the harm caused to children by its platforms to pollution produced by a factory. The money will be placed in a fund aimed at addressing the damage and preventing further harm.Meta, which owns Instagram, Facebook, WhatsApp and Threads, rejected the ruling and said it would appeal.“We disagree with the ruling and will appeal,” a Meta spokesperson said, adding that the company works to keep people safe and remains confident in its record of protecting teenagers online.The latest order follows a $375 million civil penalty previously imposed in the same case, bringing the total financial liability to $942 million.The New Mexico case began with allegations that Meta's platforms exposed young users to sexually explicit material and enabled contact with sexual predators.The court had earlier found that Meta's recommendation systems directed young users towards harmful content and contacts. In the latest phase, the judge ruled that the resulting harms met the legal threshold of a public nuisance.The judge has also ordered a series of measures aimed at limiting risks to children. These include restrictions on interactions between adults and underage users, stronger safeguards against child sexual exploitation, limits on notifications and measures to reduce excessive use of Instagram and Facebook by minors.A significant portion of the $567 million fund — $420 million — will go towards treatment and behavioural-health programmes addressing harms that have already occurred. Other money will support prevention and training for teachers and health professionals.The ruling comes as Meta faces thousands of lawsuits in the US involving alleged harms to children and teenagers. The company has also faced legal challenges over whether the design of its platforms encourages addictive use among young people.The US ruling comes at a particularly relevant moment for Meta in India, where authorities have recently scrutinised the company over child safety on Instagram.In July, India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology ordered Instagram to disable advertisements and content promoting or facilitating access to child sexual abuse material, after reports that such material had appeared in paid advertisements on the platform. The ministry also sought an explanation from Meta.Meta subsequently acknowledged reports about Instagram advertisements in India that violated its policies against child exploitation. The company said its systems had already identified and removed some of the offending advertisements and accounts, while a subsequent investigation led to further removals and blocked URLs. Meta denied that it knowingly targeted such advertisements at users based on inappropriate interests.
Article Summary: Us judge has ordered meta to pay $567m in a new mexico child safety case, ruling that instagram and facebook exposed children to harmful content and sexual exploitation. The money will be placed in a fund aimed at addressing the damage and preventing further harm.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has issued a cease and desist notices to 42 online retailers including Amazon , Walmart, Target, Wayfair and Temu parent PDD Holdings, over the sale of allegedly illegal high-speed e-bikes and e-scooters. Mamdani said that the crackdown was important to protect public safety. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Mamdani stated, “Too many lives have been cut short by high-speed, illegal e-bikes and e-scooters. That’s why we are issuing cease-and-desist orders against 42 online retailers that have been selling these dangerous devices to New York City residents — including Target, Temu, Wayfair, Walmart, and Amazon. The safety of New Yorkers is not for sale.” The city said the targeted devices exceed legal limits for speed, weight, or other safety requirements. The action follows a recent crash involving an illegal e-bike that killed a 17-year-old.According to city data, since 2017 more than 45 people have died while riding illegal e-bikes, and over 14 fatalities have been linked to crashes involving illegal stand-up scooters.Zohran Mamdani emphasised that companies profiting from such sales are putting New Yorkers at risk. “Every family deserves to know that when their loved ones leave home, they will make it back safely,” he said.Recently, Tesla CEO Elon Musk criticised New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani over his plan to open city-backed grocery stores that promise to sell some everyday food items at prices below traditional retailers. Responding to a post on X (formerly Twitter) that questioned how the proposed stores would operate, Elon Musk dismissed the plan and accused Mamdani of misleading New Yorkers. “Mamdani is a thief and a liar, plain and simple,” Musk wrote in the post. The billionaire also argued that advances in AI and robotics, rather than government-backed programmes, would eventually make goods and services much cheaper or even free.Zohran Mamdani's administration has proposed opening five city-backed grocery stores, with one planned for each of New York City's five boroughs. The city has allocated $70 million in capital funding for the programme. The first store is expected to open in Hunts Point in the Bronx by the end of 2027, followed by locations in East Harlem, Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island.Under the proposal, private grocery operators would handle day-to-day operations, including staffing, sourcing products and merchandising. The city would provide locations, cover major occupancy costs and set pricing and operating requirements. Mamdani's administration says shoppers could save about 30% on a core basket of groceries. It estimates that the programme could save an average New Yorker about $90 a month, or roughly $1,000 a year.

Their filaments were enclosed inside sealed glass bulbs, where an electric current heated the metal until it emitted visible light. However, increasing brightness also increased filament temperature, accelerating wear and shortening the bulb's lifespan.The bulb is often linked to the Phoebus Cartel, an alliance formed in 1925 by lighting companies including Philips and General Electric. Article Title: China's pharma companies are facing a 'monkey problem' that they say is as tough as 'negotiating for an Nvidia chip'
Article Text:
Lab monkeys now cost $26,294 each in China, and biotech firms say sourcing them is as hard as securing Nvidia chips.

Why lab monkey prices in China have doubled inside a year

How the monkey shortage is delaying drug trials and preclinical studies

China's lab monkey shortage runs to 2028, with Cambodia imports as the fix

In June, a Chinese state laboratory paid 178,000 yuan—about $26,294—for each of 40 cynomolgus macaques. Twelve months earlier, the same animal would have cost roughly half that. Similar spikes have rippled through the industry, according to biotech executives, and the timing could hardly be worse for a country that has spent the past five years rebuilding itself into the world's fastest drug development machine.The bottleneck is not a collapse in supply. Regulated breeding farms are holding steady. What has changed is demand, and the scale of it. China now accounts for roughly a third of the global innovative drug pipeline and is the top destination for clinical trials, and every one of those programmes needs primate safety data before it goes anywhere near a human arm. Jielun Zhu, co-founder and CFO at cancer therapy developer Excalipoint Therapeutics, compared the scramble to a large language model company chasing compute. "It's like negotiating with Nvidia to secure its chips," he said.Monkeys are the gatekeepers to the clinic, and there is no workaround. Their physiological closeness to humans makes them the most reliable surrogate for toxicology work—tracking how a drug moves through the body, what it does to organs, and whether anything about it is fatal.That matters most for biologics and newer formats such as antibody-drug conjugates, bispecifics and in vivo CAR-T, the exact areas where Chinese firms have been signing blockbuster licensing deals with Western pharma. UBS Securities' China healthcare research head Chen Chen points to those categories specifically. A single programme can consume anywhere from a dozen animals to a hundred.The practical cost is time. Harri Jarvelainen, a China-based consultant who advises Western clients on preclinical work, says study planning now takes an extra four months, and in bad cases as long as ten. Part of that is regulatory: Chinese rules require monkeys used in toxicology testing to be at least three years old, so a shortfall today cannot be bred away for another three years. Speed to clinic has been the single biggest competitive advantage Chinese biotechs hold over their American rivals, and this is the one input they cannot manufacture faster.Big contract research organisations saw this coming. WuXi AppTec, Pharmaron and Joinn Laboratories all run their own breeding operations, and Joinn in July forecast a thirteen-fold jump in first-half net profit largely because the monkeys on its books are suddenly worth so much more. Zheshang Securities estimated in February that China will run short by 15,000 to 20,000 animals annually between 2026 and 2028, with imports from Cambodia—restarted this year after a pandemic-era freeze—eventually filling part of the hole.There is precedent for the cycle. During Covid, prices went from about $1,800 a monkey in 2018 to $7,000 by 2020 as vaccine programmes piled in. This time the demand is structural, not a one-off emergency, and Zhu expects a single animal to cross 200,000 yuan next year.

China now accounts for roughly a third of the global innovative drug pipeline and is the top destination for clinical trials. China's lab monkey shortage runs to 2028, with cambodia imports as the fix.
